title: Psychology · Episode 1
chapters: Learned helplessness, and the twist fifty years later

units.t: Psychology. Episode one.
In this episode: Classical and operant conditioning, Learned helplessness, and the twist fifty years later, Psychology's most famous experiments and Personality: the Big Five.
Part one. Classical and operant conditioning.
Why does your heart jump when your phone buzzes?
Blame a Russian scientist, his dogs and a man who trained pigeons.
Pavlov's dogs.
Around 1900, Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs, work that won him a Nobel Prize in 1904.
He noticed something odd: the dogs began drooling before food arrived, at the sight of the assistants who fed them or the sound of their footsteps.
Their bodies had learned to predict food.
He then paired a neutral sound, such as a metronome or buzzer, with food.
At first the sound meant nothing.
After repeated pairings, the sound alone made the dogs salivate.
In the jargon, the food is an unconditioned stimulus because it naturally causes drooling, and the sound becomes a conditioned stimulus because it works only after learning.
That's classical conditioning.
Conditioned reactions.
Feel a jolt when your phone buzzes?
Get hungry at the rustle of a chip packet?
Feel tense in a dentist's waiting room before anything happens?
Your brain has linked a cue with an outcome.
Advertisers pair products with upbeat music and happy scenes, hoping the feeling rubs off on the brand, and a bad experience in a lift can make lifts frightening for years.
These links can fade.
If Pavlov kept sounding the buzzer without food, the drooling gradually stopped.

This is extinction, the basis of exposure therapy, one of the most effective treatments for phobias: meeting the feared cue repeatedly in safe conditions teaches the brain it no longer predicts danger.
Extinguished responses can return after a break, called spontaneous recovery, which is why old fears and habits resurface.
Learning from consequences.
In the 1930s, American psychologist B. F. Skinner studied how consequences shape behaviour.
Using boxes with levers and food dispensers, he trained rats to press levers and pigeons to peck keys, and even taught pigeons a simple version of ping-pong.
Classical conditioning links signals; operant conditioning teaches which actions pay off.
Reinforcement makes a behaviour more likely and punishment makes it less likely.
'Positive' means adding something and 'negative' means removing it.
A treat for a sitting dog is positive reinforcement.
A seatbelt beep that stops when you buckle up is negative reinforcement.
Being scolded for running late is positive punishment; losing screen time or a planned outing is negative punishment.
Rewarding what you want generally works better and lasts longer than punishing what you don't.
Unpredictable rewards.
Skinner found that rewards given unpredictably, on a variable schedule, produce the most persistent behaviour.
If a pigeon gets food every tenth peck, it pecks steadily.
If food arrives after a random number of pecks, it pecks relentlessly, and keeps going long after the food stops.
It's the logic of poker machines and social media feeds: you never know when the next reward is coming, so you keep checking.
It's also why Golden Lessons in this app appear at random.
Using it on yourself.
You can use conditioning deliberately.
Pair a habit you want with something you enjoy, like only listening to a favourite podcast while exercising.
Reward yourself immediately after the behaviour, not days later.
Notice the cues that trigger habits you don't want, like the phone on your bedside table, and remove or change them.
And be aware of variable rewards in the apps you use: turning off notifications breaks the cue, and moving apps off your home screen adds friction to the loop.
The key idea: Classical conditioning is learning to link a neutral signal with something that naturally triggers a response.
Part two. Learned helplessness, and the twist fifty years later.
A famous experiment seemed to show that animals could learn to give up.
Half a century on, the scientist who made it famous admitted they had got it backwards.
The dogs that gave up.
In 1967 Martin Seligman and Steven Maier at the University of Pennsylvania gave dogs mild but unpleasant shocks.
Some could stop the shocks by pressing a panel with their heads.
Others received exactly the same shocks but could do nothing.
Later, all the dogs were put in a box where they could escape a shock simply by jumping a low barrier.
Most dogs that had controlled the earlier shocks, or had none, quickly learned to jump.
Most of those that had faced inescapable shocks lay down and whimpered.
The researchers called this learned helplessness: the dogs had apparently learned that nothing they did mattered.
The key was not the pain but the lack of control.
Such experiments would face far tougher ethical scrutiny today.
From dogs to people.
Studies with people used milder discomforts such as noise or unsolvable puzzles.
Those who faced noise they could not switch off were often slower to find the solution later.
Seligman proposed that learned helplessness could help explain depression, in which people feel that nothing they do will make a difference.
But not everyone became helpless.
In 1978 Seligman and colleagues revised the theory to focus on how people explain bad events.
Those most at risk saw setbacks as permanent, pervasive and personal.
Those who saw them as temporary, limited and partly due to circumstances bounced back more readily.
This work fed into learned optimism, positive psychology and cognitive therapies that help people question their automatic explanations.
The twist.
Steven Maier, by then a neuroscientist, traced the brain circuits behind the original effect.
In 2016 he and Seligman published a paper looking back at fifty years of work.
They reported that the original theory had the mechanism backwards.
Passivity in the face of prolonged bad events is not learned.
It is the brain's default response, driven by a deep brainstem region called the dorsal raphe nucleus.
What can be learned is control.
When an animal discovers that its actions work, a region of the prefrontal cortex detects this and switches off the default passivity.
In other words, it is not helplessness we learn, but hope.
Control builds resilience.
Maier's experiments in rats found that animals that first experienced controllable stress were later more resilient, even when facing stress they could not control.
The experience of mastery seemed to leave a lasting protective effect, at least in those studies.
The findings are mainly from animals, so care is needed in applying them to people.
Still, they fit human research suggesting that a sense of agency matters for wellbeing.

They suggest the best defence against hopelessness may not be avoiding hardship altogether, but building genuine experiences of effort paying off, so the brain has evidence that what we do can make a difference.
Science correcting itself.
The phrase learned helplessness is now part of everyday language, and the basic observation has held up well: repeated uncontrollable setbacks can sap motivation.
What changed was the explanation of why.
It is a fine example of science working properly, with the original scientists revising their own famous theory when better evidence arrived.
The practical message is encouraging.
If giving up is the default, small, achievable wins are not trivial.

Breaking a big problem into manageable steps, noticing what you can influence, and questioning explanations that are permanent, pervasive and personal are all ways of teaching the brain, again and again, that effort matters.
The key idea: Dogs given shocks they could not control often failed to escape later, when escape was easy.
Part three. Psychology's most famous experiments.
Prisons in basements, summer-camp feuds and fake patients.
The studies everyone's heard of, and what they really showed.
Famous isn't solid.
Some psychology experiments became famous because they told a striking story: that ordinary people can turn cruel, or that rival groups turn hostile as soon as they compete.
They shape textbooks, films and how people think about human nature.
But since the early 2010s psychology has faced a 'replication crisis'.
In a major 2015 project, teams repeated 100 published studies and got clearly similar results in well under half of them.
Good signs in research include large samples, pre-registered methods, a public plan made in advance, shared data and results that independent teams reproduce.
Looking closely at famous studies teaches two lessons at once: what they suggest about people, and how careful good science needs to be.
Stories that unravelled.
In 1971, Philip Zimbardo turned a Stanford basement into a mock prison, with male student volunteers randomly assigned as guards or prisoners.
Some guards became cruel and the study stopped after six days.
It was long used to argue that situations alone turn good people bad.
Later investigations found guards were encouraged to be tough and some behaviour was performed for the researchers.
A 2002 BBC prison study saw no guard tyranny.
In 1973, David Rosenhan reported that eight healthy people went to 12 US psychiatric hospitals claiming to hear voices saying 'empty' and 'hollow'.
All were admitted and stayed about 19 days.
In 2019, journalist Susannah Cahalan found details that didn't match his notes, and she could trace only two of the pseudopatients.
Robbers Cave.
In 1954, Muzafer Sherif took 22 boys aged about 11 to a summer camp at Robbers Cave State Park in Oklahoma.
They were split into two groups, the Eagles and the Rattlers, which bonded separately before meeting.
A tournament with prizes only for the winners soon led to name-calling, flag burning and cabin raids.
Simply sharing meals and films did little to help.
What worked were problems, quietly arranged by staff, that needed both groups, such as a blocked water supply and a stalled food truck.
By the end, many friendships crossed group lines.
Shared goals are still used to ease conflict.
But in 2018 Gina Perry described an abandoned 1953 trial in which the boys realised adults were stirring up trouble and turned on the staff instead.
Ethics and attachment.
Two classics show why ethics rules exist.
John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner wanted to show that fear could be learned.
They struck a steel bar behind an infant, known as Little Albert, whenever he reached for a white rat.
Soon he cried at the rat and seemed wary of similar furry things.
It supported classical conditioning in humans, but it involved one child, was poorly documented, and his fear was never removed.
Even his identity is debated.
In the 1950s, Harry Harlow raised infant rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers: bare wire with milk, or soft cloth without.
The babies clung to the cloth mother and visited the wire one mainly to feed.
Attachment isn't just about food.
But isolated monkeys were badly harmed, fuelling debate about animal research.
A study that held up.
Not every famous study has crumbled.
In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed people a film of a car crash, then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' or 'hit' each other.
The 'smashed' group gave higher estimates.
A week later, about a third of them said they had seen broken glass, compared with roughly one in seven of the 'hit' group.
There was none.
Research on misleading questions has been repeated many times and has changed how police are advised to interview witnesses.
Classical conditioning and the spacing effect also replicate well.
When you hear 'a study shows', ask how many people took part, whether anyone has repeated it, and whether the story sounds a little too neat.
The key idea: Famous studies deserve scrutiny, because psychology's replication crisis showed that striking findings often don't hold up when repeated.
Part four. Personality: the Big Five.
Forget star signs and most online quizzes.
Psychologists measure personality with five traits, and they predict real things about your life.
Five broad traits.
When people describe themselves and others, the words cluster into a few broad dimensions.
Decades of research across many cultures settled on five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, remembered as OCEAN.
Each is a spectrum, not a box, and most people sit near the middle on most traits.
The model grew from the lexical hypothesis: if a difference matters, languages will have words for it.
In 1936, Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert found about 18,000 English words describing people.
Statistics boiled them down to the same five clusters, and questionnaires built in the 1980s and 90s are still used.
Scores stay similar on retest and predict real outcomes, from job performance to health.
Some researchers argue for a sixth factor, honesty-humility.
Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion.
People high in openness love new ideas, art, travel and abstract thinking; lower scorers prefer the familiar and practical.
Openness is linked to creativity and, on average, more liberal attitudes.
Conscientiousness means being organised, reliable and hardworking.

It is among the best personality predictors of success at school and work, and it is linked to better health and a longer life, perhaps because conscientious people exercise, avoid risks and follow medical advice.
Very high levels can tip into perfectionism and inflexibility.
Extraverts are talkative, energetic and energised by company, and tend to feel more positive emotion.
Introverts prefer quieter settings and recharge alone.
That differs from shyness, which is anxiety about social judgement.
Agreeableness and neuroticism.
Agreeableness describes kindness, trust, modesty and cooperation.
Highly agreeable people avoid conflict and put others first; lower scorers are more competitive, sceptical and blunt.
Neither end is simply good: a negotiator, critic or auditor may benefit from lower agreeableness.
People high in neuroticism, or low in emotional stability, feel stress, worry, sadness and irritation more often and more intensely.
Low scorers stay calm under pressure.
High neuroticism is linked to a higher risk of anxiety and depression, but it isn't a diagnosis, and its caution can help, such as noticing risks others miss.
Exercise, good sleep and cognitive behavioural therapy can help manage it.
If worry or low mood is affecting daily life, a GP is a good first step.
Prediction and change.
Personality isn't destiny, but it adds up.
A well-known 2007 review by Brent Roberts and colleagues found that traits predicted how long people live, divorce and career success about as well as family income or intelligence did.
Conscientiousness predicts job performance in most occupations, and lower neuroticism and higher agreeableness go with more satisfying relationships.
Each link is modest for one person, but the patterns are consistent.
Twin studies suggest roughly 40-60 per cent of the variation between people is linked to genes, yet personality isn't fixed.
From young adulthood to middle age, people tend to become more conscientious and agreeable and less neurotic, the 'maturity principle'.
Specific goals and repeated practice can shift traits gradually.
What about Myers-Briggs.
The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator was developed in the 1940s by Katharine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers, based on Carl Jung's ideas.
It sorts people into 16 types, like INTJ or ESFP, and is popular in workplaces.
But psychologists criticise it.
It forces people into either-or categories when most sit near the middle, and many people get a different type when retested weeks later.
Star signs don't predict personality at all in studies.
If you're curious, a free Big Five test from a university research site is a more accurate mirror.
The key idea: Decades of research settled on five broad personality spectrums, remembered as OCEAN, that stay stable on retest and predict real outcomes.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did Pavlov's dogs begin to salivate at the buzzer?
Answer. They had learned that the sound predicted food.
Question two. What mattered most in the original dog experiments?
Answer. Lack of control over the shocks.
Question three. What does psychology's 'replication crisis' mean for famous studies?
Answer. Many findings didn't hold up when others repeated them.
Question four. Why are the Big Five traits described as spectrums?
Answer. Most people sit near the middle of each scale.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
